opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it's been really encouraging, and it's shifted a lot in just the last couple of years. If you'd asked mathematicians five years ago, I think many would have said formal verification was a niche thing, interesting to a small group of people but too tedious to matter for working mathematicians. Writing a proof in Lean meant spelling out every tiny step the computer needed, steps a human would wave through with "clearly" or "it's easy to see."

What's changed is a combination of things. First, Mathlib, the community-built library of formalized mathematics, has grown enormously, so you're no longer starting from scratch. Second, a few very prominent mathematicians publicly embraced it. When people like Terence Tao start formalizing results and talking openly about how useful it is, that gives a lot of legitimacy. And third, AI is starting to take away the tedium. If a system can fill in the routine steps, Lean stops being a burden and becomes a superpower.

That said, there's a healthy skepticism, and I think that's appropriate. Mathematicians care deeply about understanding, not just about getting a checkmark that something is true. So a common reaction is: "Great, the machine says it's correct, but does it help me understand why?" That's a fair question, and it's one we think about a lot. Our view is that verification and understanding aren't in tension. If you know a proof is correct, you can spend your energy on interpreting it and building intuition, rather than worrying about whether there's a subtle error on page forty.

There's also an important trust dimension with AI specifically. People have seen language models confidently produce nonsense, so there's a natural wariness about AI-generated math. That's exactly why we think pairing AI with Lean matters so much. You don't have to trust the model. You trust the checker, which is small, well understood, and auditable. That reframes the whole conversation. It's not "believe the AI," it's "the AI did the work and the proof checks."

So overall, I'd say the reception has gone from curiosity to genuine engagement. Younger mathematicians especially are growing up with these tools, and I expect that within a decade it'll seem normal for significant results to come with a formal proof, much like it's normal now to typeset papers in LaTeX.

r001.rationale: The response says younger mathematicians are growing up with these tools, but does not compare their receptiveness with older mathematicians.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's been one of the more interesting shifts I've watched over the last few years. If you'd asked me in, say, 2022, I'd have told you the mathematics community was broadly skeptical, and for good reason. Mathematicians care about understanding, not just about whether a statement is true. A proof is supposed to tell you why something holds. So the fear was that AI would produce these inscrutable artifacts that are technically correct but teach you nothing.

What's changed the conversation is Lean specifically, and the fact that formal verification sidesteps the trust problem entirely. You don't have to trust the model. You don't have to trust us. If the proof type-checks against Mathlib, it's correct, full stop. That turns out to matter enormously to mathematicians, because the alternative, a language model confidently asserting a proof in natural language, is exactly the thing they find most irritating. Hallucinated lemmas, hand-waved steps. Lean removes that failure mode.

So the reception has split a bit. There's a group, people like Kevin Buzzard, Terence Tao, folks who've been formalizing for a while, who were already bought in and see AI as the thing that finally makes formalization scale. Formalizing a paper used to cost months of expert labor. If a model can do the tedious parts, that changes what's feasible.

Then there's a larger group who were indifferent to Lean before and are now paying attention precisely because AI made it relevant. They don't want to write Lean themselves, and honestly they shouldn't have to. But they're interested in a world where they can sketch an argument and have the gaps filled and checked.

And there's still a skeptical camp, which I actually think is healthy. Their concern is less "will this work" and more "what does it do to the culture." Does mathematics become a game of hitting formal targets? Do we lose the informal, intuitive side? I take that seriously. My view is that verification should be the floor, not the ceiling. It tells you a result is true. The interesting part, the explanation and the new ideas, is still the human part, at least for now.

The most encouraging thing to me is that the conversation has moved from "should we trust this" to "what should we do with it." That's a very different place than where we were a few years ago.

r001.rationale: The response describes groups of mathematicians with differing levels of interest and skepticism, but it does not compare younger mathematicians with older mathematicians or say that younger mathematicians are generally more receptive.

astra-6.text:
I think there are two different questions: how mathematicians feel about AI generating mathematics, and how they feel about tools like Lean checking mathematics. Those don’t necessarily get the same reception.

With AI, the skepticism is understandable. Something can look like a convincing proof and still have a subtle gap. Lean offers a way to check whether a formal proof follows from the stated definitions and assumptions. That makes it possible to separate how an argument was discovered from whether it checks out.

But correctness is only part of what mathematicians care about. They also want insight: why something is true, what connections it reveals, whether it leads to an interesting new question. And formalizing an argument takes work. So I think adoption depends on these tools becoming useful enough that the benefit outweighs that effort. Helping someone get past a genuine obstacle in their research is a much stronger case than simply saying the technology is impressive.

r001.rationale: The response discusses skepticism, Lean’s role, and adoption generally, but does not compare younger and older mathematicians’ receptiveness.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the mathematics community is curious, but understandably skeptical. If an AI produces a proof that looks convincing, that’s not enough—you still have to know whether every step is correct. And checking a plausible but subtly wrong proof can take a lot of work.

That’s where something like Lean becomes really interesting. You can separate the process of finding a proof, which might involve an unreliable AI, from checking the proof, which is done by a small, precise verifier. You don’t have to trust the model’s explanation.

But correctness isn’t the only thing mathematicians care about. They also want understanding: why is this true, what’s the important idea, how does it connect to other things? So I think reception will depend on whether these tools help people do mathematics they care about, and whether they fit into the way mathematicians actually work.

r001.rationale: The response describes mathematicians as curious but skeptical overall; it does not compare younger and older mathematicians or say younger mathematicians are more receptive.
